scenes.text: Come close, baby, this fire don't reach far. They want me to talk into that little machine. A hundred and six years old... alright then. Let me reach back and get it for you. All of it.

scenes.text: Greenwood. North side of Tulsa. White folks called it Black Wall Street. We just called it ours. Every face on that street knew your mama. That's the part no book ever got right.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, ornate theater marquee lit at dusk on a brick main street
scenes.text: We had a hotel so fine the floors talked back when you walked. A picture theater with seats clean to the back of forever. And a piano somewhere going all night long. Lord, that piano.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, shopkeeper hands passing a dollar bill across a worn wooden counter, general store shelves
scenes.text: A dollar didn't leave our neighborhood in a hurry. It went from the barber to the grocer to the church plate, taking its sweet time. Daddy said that's what respect looks like when it circulates.

scenes.text: My daddy doctored folks up a narrow stair, his name in gold paint on the glass. Smelled like iodine and peppermint up there. Mama nursed beside him when she wasn't nursing me.

scenes.text: I was eight. Had one good ribbon and patent shoes that pinched like a crawdad. In the one photograph we saved, somebody tinted my ribbon pink by hand. I loved that ribbon more than some people.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, rows of new brick buildings with scaffolds, morning light, builders at work in the distance
scenes.text: Daddy used to say Greenwood got built twice. Once inside somebody's head, once in brick. Took me eighty years to understand him. Everything you ever seen started out as a dream somebody kept.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, American flags on quiet storefronts, closed shop signs, empty morning street
scenes.text: Monday. Memorial Day. Must have been the last of May, because the flags was out and the stores was shut. Now hold my hand through this next part, baby. This is where it turns.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival photograph, young Black man at a shoeshine stand, warm grin, customer shoe on the brass rest
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, young Black man at a shoeshine stand, warm grin, customer shoe on the brass rest
scenes.text: There was a boy shined shoes downtown. Everybody called him Diamond Dick. Pretty boy. Grin like he owed you money and knew you'd forgive him. His given name? Gone, child. The grin stayed.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, tall downtown office building, stone facade and revolving door, pedestrians in boaters
scenes.text: A colored man couldn't use just any washroom downtown. The one they left us sat at the top of a tall building, and you rode a little elevator to get there. That's all that boy went to do. Ride up. Come down.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival photograph, ornate brass scissor-gate elevator interior, operator stool, overhead lamp, empty
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, ornate brass scissor-gate elevator interior, operator stool, overhead lamp, empty
scenes.text: A girl ran that elevator. Young. White. I never learned her name long enough to forget it. Two children in a brass box, and history squeezing in there with them. It's a small room, history. Fits anywhere.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, elevator floor indicator dial above closed doors, dramatic shadow
scenes.text: The car jumped. He stumbled. His hand caught her arm, the way you'd catch anybody. And she hollered. And he ran. Because a colored boy in that town knew arithmetic, and a holler was a number too big.

scenes.text: A clerk next door heard the scream and let his imagination finish the story. That's all it took, sugar. One man's imagination. Fear writes fast, and it don't stop to check its spelling.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival photograph, police station front desk, open ledger book, officer cap resting on the counter
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, police station front desk, open ledger book, officer cap resting on the counter
scenes.text: Now here's what they don't tell you. The police wasn't even sure anything happened. The girl wouldn't swear to nothing. On any honest day, that's where it dies. It just wasn't going to be an honest day.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, dusk over district rooftops, chimneys and a church steeple, warm amber sky
scenes.text: That night we slept easy under our own roofs. You don't know a sleep is precious till you count how few of them you got left. That was the last easy one for a long, long while.

scenes.text: Tuesday morning they came got Diamond Dick anyway, quiet, and set him in the courthouse jail. The sheriff, Mac-something, big square man, held them keys honest. Remember him kind, whoever he was.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, evening street with lit shop windows, cafe chairs, a broom leaning on a doorframe
scenes.text: Greenwood didn't know one thing yet. Supper going, piano tuning up, men sweeping their own doorsteps. We was rich the way that counts, baby. We belonged to each other. You hear me? Belonged.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival photograph, newspaper building at dusk, tall lit windows, newsprint rolls stacked at the dock
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, newspaper building at dusk, tall lit windows, newsprint rolls stacked at the dock
scenes.text: But downtown there was an afternoon paper needed selling. And there is no cheaper kindling on God's green earth than a white girl's scream and a Black boy's name set in the same line of type.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, linotype machine closeup, rows of metal type, operator hands at the keys
scenes.text: I can't quote you the headline. I was eight years old. But grown folks said it plain. The paper all but printed an invitation. Come to the courthouse tonight. Bring your rope.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival photograph, newspaper with a ragged torn-out column on dark wood beside a lamp
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, newspaper with a ragged torn-out column on dark wood beside a lamp
scenes.text: And here is the part that makes my hands cold. Go look for that page today. Torn out. Every copy, every archive, one careful hand. Paper can be cut, baby. What I carry can't.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival photograph, newsboys with paper bundles on a corner, men in hats reaching for copies
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, newsboys with paper bundles on a corner, men in hats reaching for copies
scenes.text: Papers hit the street middle of the afternoon. Newsboys hollering it corner to corner. Folks said you could stand on our side of the tracks and feel it coming. Like weather. Like a green sky.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival photograph, empty town square at dusk, long shadows, courthouse in the distance
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, empty town square at dusk, long shadows, courthouse in the distance
scenes.text: By suppertime the talk downtown was rope. They had lynched a white boy in that same town not a year before, and the law just watched it happen. Everybody knew the recipe worked. Everybody.

scenes.text: Come dark they was collecting at the courthouse. Hundreds first. Then more than I got numbers for. And that sheriff, bless him, barred his own doors and told that crowd one word. No.

scenes.text: And down our way, men who had soldiered in France set down their suppers and stood up. Some still had the Army coat. If the law couldn't hold the line, they would. That's not rage, child. That's arithmetic.

scenes.text: Daddy locked the office early. Mama held my hand too tight the whole walk home, and I taste copper just telling it. The air had changed. You could feel tomorrow coming, and it was coming armed.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival photograph, single revolver lying on stone courthouse steps in lamplight
scenes.text: One gun is going to go off outside that courthouse, baby. Nobody will ever know whose finger. And the whole world is going to tear its shirt. But that's tomorrow's telling, not tonight's.
